strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: enabling high-resolution self-supervised pretraining on consumer-grade hardware, relevant for privacy-constrained research environments
Comprehensive ablation studies systematically validating design choices (downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, masking strategy) across multiple resolutions
Impressive empirical efficiency gains: 7× FLOP reduction and 2× memory savings at 768×768 resolution with minimal performance loss (0.4% mIoU difference)
Well-grounded masking strategy: Perlin masking validated through spectral analysis aligned with biological signal properties
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, explicit hyperparameters, standard hardware specifications, and clear training procedures
Effective combination of techniques: thoughtfully integrates adaptive token merging, deep supervision, numerically stable kernels, and point-based decoding into coherent system
Good data efficiency: demonstrates superior generalization with limited training data (5% shows 0.3910 vs 0.2529 mIoU advantage)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: individual components (hierarchical downsampling, deep supervision, Perlin noise) are not novel; contribution is primarily engineering-focused
Narrow evaluation scope: single domain (Electron Microscopy), small dataset (570 training images), only 4 semantic classes; generalization to other domains and standard benchmarks unclear

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons with other efficient pretraining methods, hierarchical vision transformers, and recent efficient MAE variants; baseline ViT-MAE not optimized for efficiency

Insufficient justification of design choices: why Perlin masking works relies on biological intuition rather than rigorous validation; softmax interpolation justification is ad-hoc; decoder design rationale underdeveloped
Shallow analysis of deep supervision: mechanistic explanation of why it prevents representation collapse is superficial; unclear if necessary specifically for this architecture or general requirement
Overstated scalability claims: efficiency gains demonstrated primarily for EM imaging; no exploration beyond 768×768 resolution or domain-specific pretraining effects on transfer learning
Missing sensitivity analyses: Perlin noise parameter sensitivity, convergence dynamics, batch size effects, and hardware generalization not explored
Lack of theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of why this specific combination is optimal; numerical stability improvements practical but theoretically unmotivated
Limited dataset availability: in-house FPF dataset not publicly available; domain-specific EM pretraining may limit general feature learning; 187K unlabeled images modest by modern standards
Dense technical presentation: Sections 3.2-3.3 with complex notation could be clearer; PCA visualization (Figure 4) is qualitative; no discussion of failure modes

strengths: Addresses practical problem of high-resolution pretraining on consumer GPUs with systematic engineering solutions and achieves significant efficiency gains (7× FLOP, 2× memory reduction)
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 2a-2d) systematically validate each component's contribution to performance
Demonstrates strong data efficiency with high performance (≥0.59 mIoU) using only 5% of labeled training data, suggesting learned representations generalize within the domain
Technically sound implementation with proper mathematical formulations and principled analysis of feature collapse via Normalized Effective Rank
Practical value demonstrated for resource-constrained settings with end-to-end training speedups and memory efficiency
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: entire assessment uses single domain (electron microscopy) with tiny dataset (570 train/164 test images); no evaluation on standard benchmarks (ImageNet, COCO, Cityscapes) making generalizability claims completely unsupported

Negligible or negative performance gains: at 512 resolution AFFMAE achieves 0.6030 mIoU vs. 0.6054 for ViT-MAE baseline (0.4% degradation), contradicting claimed superiority and questioning practical utility of added complexity

Narrow baseline comparisons missing critical related work: only ViT and ViT-MAE evaluated; no comparisons with hierarchical transformers (Swin, PVT, DeiT), other efficiency methods (distillation, pruning), or domain-specific pretraining approaches

Limited technical novelty: paper primarily combines existing techniques (AutoFocusFormer, MAE, token merging, deep supervision) with primary contribution being Perlin masking justified only through EM-specific spectral analysis without general theoretical grounding

Questionable generalizability of design choices: Perlin masking strategy relies on 1/f spectral characteristics unique to EM images; hyperparameters appear dataset-tuned without principled justification for transfer to other domains
Missing reproducibility elements: no code availability, reliance on specific NVIDIA hardware version, incomplete Perlin noise generation specifications limit verification and adoption

Insufficient theoretical justification: connection between Normalized Effective Rank maintenance and downstream performance assumed but not validated; why spectral characteristics should drive general-purpose pretraining masking unexplained

strengths: Addresses a practical problem that limits adoption of self-supervised learning in resource-constrained settings, enabling high-resolution pretraining on consumer-grade GPUs
Comprehensive experimental validation with thorough ablation studies examining downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, and masking strategy

Solid technical execution: numerically stable softmax interpolation, adaptive off-grid token merging, and effective integration of auxiliary losses (deep supervision with normalized effective rank validation)
Achieves significant efficiency gains (7× FLOP reduction, 2× memory reduction, 36% wall-clock speedup) while maintaining competitive performance on the target task
Well-motivated design choices supported by analysis: Perlin masking rationale (Figure 7), effective rank monitoring (Figure 5), and data efficiency insights (Figure 11)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and generally sound mathematical exposition
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to a single specialized domain (electron microscopy) with only one downstream task; generalization to natural images and other modalities remains unclear
Modest performance improvement over baseline (0.4% mIoU gain at 512×512), raising questions about whether domain-specific engineering justifies the contribution for broader applicability

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing experiments with other hierarchical models (e.g., Swin+MAE), recent efficient transformers (DeiT), and other GPU-efficient pretraining methods mentioned in related work
Limited algorithmic novelty: AFFMAE primarily combines existing components (AutoFocusFormer + MAE) without introducing fundamental innovations; contribution is primarily engineering-focused

Insufficient justification for several design choices: Perlin masking strategy lacks theoretical grounding beyond intuition, softmax temperature sensitivity not analyzed, unclear why AutoFocusFormer specifically is optimal

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, mixed-precision CUDA kernel and Triton implementation details incomplete, insufficient specification for reproduction outside the authors' environment
Narrow experimental scope limits impact assessment: single dataset, single task, no cross-domain transfer experiments, no comparison to standard benchmarks where published results exist

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: enables privacy-preserving in-domain pretraining on consumer hardware for resource-constrained labs—a genuine bottleneck in biomedical research.

Comprehensive technical execution with engineering rigor: numerical stability improvements for inverse-distance weighting, Flash-style attention kernels, quantized KNN lookup caching yielding measurable speedups.
Extensive empirical validation: thorough ablations (Table 1), evaluation on multiple public EM datasets beyond proprietary data, proper error bars across 4 seeds.

Principled analysis of design choices: Normalized Effective Rank quantifies representational collapse, spectral analysis elegantly justifies Perlin masking via 1/f statistics, visualizations confirm adaptive merging behavior.
Significant practical efficiency gains: 2× pretraining speedup, 2× memory reduction (14.5 vs 29.7 GB), 5× fine-tuning speedup at 1024px while maintaining parity with ViT-MAE accuracy.
Superior handling of fine-grained structures: outperforms grid-aligned hierarchical methods on small filtration slits (0.514 vs 0.447 IoU) due to adaptive token retention.
Honest discussion of limitations: clearly identifies memory traffic overhead, cache scaling limits (~1200px), and open challenges for volumetric extension.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily engineering existing components (AutoFocusFormer, Deep Supervision, Perlin noise) together; no novel vision model insights or theoretical contributions.

Application-specific focus limits broader impact: extensive optimization for kidney EM foot-process-width only; public evaluations use same EM modality; generalization to other microscopy/imaging domains unexplored.

Incomplete hardware-matched comparisons: GreenMIM/HiViT/MixMAE trained on H100 while AFFMAE on RTX 5090, making speedup attribution ambiguous (method vs. hardware). Recommendation: rerun baselines on same GPU.

Unresolved technical questions: (1) Why does aggressive downsampling cause representational collapse only in off-grid architectures? Would grid-based hierarchical models suffer similarly? (2) Loss weighting scheme for deep supervision never specified—critical for reproducibility. (3) Space-filling curve clustering procedure referenced but not detailed; no ablation on alternatives.

Masking strategy generalization unclear: Perlin masking at 50% ratio outperforms random at 75% in EM but domain-specificity unexplored; no evaluation on natural images where random masking is standard baseline.

Acknowledged scalability limitations under-addressed: dense lookup tables exceed cache >~1200px, grid indexing becomes competitive; volumetric extension requires 'open challenges' in clustering/lookup/masking—limits future applicability.
Reproducibility gaps: code link incomplete in abstract; custom Triton kernels non-trivial to reproduce; CLAHE preprocessing impact not ablated.
Statistical clarity issues: some differences within error bars (Lucchi++: 0.8840±? vs 0.8829±?); no significance testing; FPW MAE metric differences may lack medical significance.

Missing failure mode analysis: no discussion of when AFFMAE underperforms baselines, which structures benefit least from adaptive downsampling, or when practitioners should prefer standard MAE despite resource cost.
Incomplete baseline coverage: no CNN-based U-Net/ResU-Net comparisons standard in medical imaging; nnU-Net V2 uses sliding-window inference + ensembling (acknowledged as unfair but included anyway).

strengths: Addresses a real practical problem: enabling in-domain high-resolution pretraining for labs with privacy constraints and limited server infrastructure

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple public benchmarks (Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, ISBI) with thorough ablation studies on key components (downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, masking strategy)
Strong analytical validation including PCA visualization of representational collapse, Normalized Effective Rank analysis justifying deep supervision, and spectral analysis of masking strategies
Solid engineering optimizations: numerically stable softmax reformulation for inverse-power weighting, Flash-style cluster attention in Triton, and cached KNN lookup with measured 1.5× speedup
Achieves performance parity with ViT-MAE while reducing pretraining time by 2× and halving fine-tuning memory overhead on consumer GPU hardware
Token visualization demonstrates interpretable adaptive downsampling behavior concentrating on information-rich regions (e.g., biological membranes)
Good reproducibility support: code promised, hyperparameters detailed in appendix, results reported with standard deviations across 4 seeds
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily combines existing components (AutoFocusFormer [38], standard MAE [13], deformable attention [37], deep supervision [18], Perlin noise [23]). Main contributions are engineering optimizations (Triton kernels, cached KNN lookup) rather than algorithmic advances

Unfair experimental comparisons: baselines (GreenMIM, HiViT, MixMAE) trained on H100 while AFFMAE on RTX 5090 with different batch sizes, making wall-clock time comparisons fundamentally problematic and acknowledged but unresolved

Deep supervision is a critical dependency showing 3% performance collapse without auxiliary losses (0.5908→0.5734), suggesting AFF+MAE is inherently unstable. This appears as a workaround rather than principled solution, and unclear if baselines use equivalent supervision
Efficiency-accuracy mismatch: GFLOPs reduced ~4× but throughput only ~2× faster, indicating memory bandwidth remains bottleneck. Gap between theoretical and realized speedups inadequately addressed

Accuracy gains are marginal and within noise: Lucchi++ (−0.0011), Kasthuri++ (+0.0052), ISBI (+0.0012). Paper achieves parity with MAE, not improvements, making efficiency rather than accuracy the selling point

Overly domain-specific scope: focused exclusively on kidney EM for foot process width measurement. Applicability to general high-resolution vision tasks (remote sensing, pathology, natural images) undemonstrated. Better suited to specialized biomedical venues (MIDL, MICCAI) than ECCV

Weak Perlin masking contribution: marginal empirical improvement (0.5947→0.6009, Δ=0.0062) with unclear generalization beyond specialized EM domain. Spectral justification is motivational but not sufficient for novelty claim

Problematic experimental setup: primary FPW dataset tiny (570 train/235 test images); in-domain vs. ImageNet pretraining comparison (0.476→0.606) expected and not novel; confounds dataset size and pretraining method effects due to different scales (1.28M vs. 187k images)

Incomplete comparisons: no comparison with knowledge distillation for efficient pretraining; no analysis of whether lower-resolution MAE (512×512) would suffice for many applications; unclear when 1024× pretraining is truly necessary

Presentation tries to cover too much (adaptive downsampling, MAE integration, deep supervision, Perlin masking, Triton kernels, applications), diluting core contribution identification. Public dataset results relegated to appendix
Limited transferability analysis: no demonstration on non-microscopy high-resolution tasks; unclear if insights generalize to natural images or other computer vision domains

Acknowledged but unresolved gap: irregular token sets complicate cache efficiency and bandwidth; dense lookup tables may exceed cache capacity at very high resolutions; irregular addressing hurts memory efficiency compared to dense grid indexing

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses genuine constraints (compute, data governance) preventing in-domain pretraining in biomedical labs, with clear motivation for kidney EM as a challenging domain

Technically sound engineering: numerically stable exponential-kernel replacement for mixed precision, Flash-style Triton kernels, clever cached KNN lookup optimization (1.4-1.5× speedups), all implementationally solid

Rigorous experimental evaluation: comprehensive ablations isolating each component, multi-resolution evaluation (512/768/1024px), results with standard deviations across 4 seeds, evaluation on 4 public benchmarks demonstrating some generalization

Substantial practical efficiency gains: matches ViT-MAE accuracy (0.633 mIoU @1024px) while achieving 2× pretraining speedup, 5× finetuning speedup, ~2× memory reduction; scales to 896px where baselines OOM

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear problem setup, effective visualizations (Fig 6b token merging, Fig 2b effective rank, Fig 3b spectral analysis), detailed supplementary material, honest discussion of limitations

Strong validation of design choices: Perlin masking justified via spectral analysis aligning with natural image statistics, Deep Supervision validated with normalized effective rank analysis, in-domain pretraining importance demonstrated empirically (0.494 → 0.606)
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: core contribution combines existing AutoFocusFormer [38] + MAE [13]; combination is natural rather than innovative; novelty primarily in engineering (Triton kernels) rather than new concepts

Uncertain generalization beyond microscopy: method heavily tuned for kidney EM (Perlin masking for 1/f statistics, deep supervision for sparse stages, specific downsampling rates); improvements on public benchmarks marginal (0.8829 vs 0.8840 Lucchi++, 0.8661 vs 0.8649 ISBI); no natural image experiments

Deep Supervision as architectural band-aid: critical for performance (+3% at ds=0.4) but feels ad-hoc; effective rank analysis provided but limited investigation into root causes of collapse in sparse hierarchical layers; adds complexity without addressing fundamental design

Incomplete experimental comparisons: missing recent efficient ViTs (MobileViT, EfficientViT); hardware differences for baselines (H100 vs RTX 5090) affect timing fairness; nnUNet uses different techniques (sliding windows, ensembling) making direct comparison problematic

Acknowledged scalability limitations not addressed: lookup tables exceed cache at >1200px resolution, bandwidth limitations from gather/scatter operations remain, constraints treated as future work rather than solved

Limited theoretical insight: connection between adaptive off-grid token merging and MAE efficiency is intuitive but not formalized; no analysis of why AutoFocusFormer specifically solves masking-friendly design or comparison with other sparse architectures

Reproducibility concerns: code link incomplete in paper, many hyperparameters tuned (downsampling rates, masking ratios, neighborhood sizes), unclear methodology for hyperparameter selection across FPW vs. public benchmarks

Minimal analysis of learned representations: PCA visualizations (Fig 2a) difficult to interpret, no quantitative characterization of what is learned beyond segmentation tasks, token concentration analysis qualitative only
